bib.title: Skill-MAS: Evolving Meta-Skill for Automatic Multi-Agent Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Skill-MAS: Evolving Meta-Skill for Automatic Multi-Agent Systems", Hehai Lin, Qi Yang, Chengwei Qin (Ant Group; HKUST-Guangzhou). arXiv 2606.18837v3 [cs.MA], 29 Sep 2026. Preprint (no venue printed).

COVERAGE: Read about 70,000 of 155,077 chars in full (abstract through Appendix D.4, Tables 1-8, the start of Appendix E, the initial Meta-Skill in Fig. 5, and the start of the Fig. 6 skill text). Also read the Table 9 BrowseComp-Plus MAS comparison and the full figure-caption list. NOT read, about 85k chars: the optimized Meta-Skill texts (Figs 6-14, bar the first lines of Fig. 6 and the tail of Fig. 14), the VitaBench part of the Table 9/10 case study, and the prompts (Figs 15-21, pp. 28-34). I did not extract that remainder, so nothing from it appears below. The references were skimmed for origins only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Skill-MAS evolves a text "Meta-Skill" (a SKILL.md-style document) for a frozen Meta-agent that writes the multi-agent system (MAS). It improves average accuracy over five automatic-MAS baselines on all four models.
  number: optimized avg perf 29.49 / 27.55 / 38.41 / 41.05 (Gemini / GPT / Qwen / DeepSeek). Best baseline avg is 21.29 (AFlow) / 24.83 (EvoAgent) / 32.23 (AFlow) / 35.70 (AFlow).
  setup: Meta-agent and all components use the same LLM: Gemini-3.1-Flash and GPT-5.4-Nano (low reasoning effort), Qwen3.5-Plus and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Benchmarks are DeepResearchBench, HLE-Math, BrowseComp-Plus and VitaBench. Held-out test sets are 84/168/168/84 items. R=10 rounds, K=5 rollouts. Single table, no variance reported.
  quote: "In all other cases, Skill-MAS-optimized outperforms all baseline methods by a large margin and achieves the highest average performance across all LLMs."
  where: Sec 5.1, Table 1 (~chars 19000-22500)
- The one per-cell exception is DeepResearchBench with GPT-5.4-Nano. Skill-MAS-optimized scores 48.90 and EvoAgent 52.91, though the paper's wording is garbled.
  quote: "the only exception occurs on DeepResearchBench with GPT-5.4-Nano, where EvoAgent maintains a higher advantage (48.90 vs. 52.91)"
  where: Sec 5.1
- The unevolved initial skill is already competitive. It is a generic 3-module prompt distilled by an LLM from Anthropic (2026), "Building multi-agent systems: when and how to use them".
  number: Gemini 21.68 vs best baseline 21.29. Init is below the best baseline on GPT (19.64 vs 24.83) and Qwen (32.61 vs 32.23, slightly above). DeepSeek 33.72 is below AFlow's 35.70.
  quote: "Skill-MAS-init slightly surpasses the best baseline AFlow (21.68 vs. 21.29)"
  where: Sec 5.1
- Cost: the paper claims a better cost-performance trade-off because the MAS is generated in one shot. Training-time methods are cheapest but worst. Inference-time search methods (EvoAgent, AFlow, AOrchestra) are costly per query. Skill-MAS is "moderate". Reported inference cost on the test set is not the lowest.
  number: Skill-MAS-optimized avg cost 2.82 / 5.22 / 2.43 / 2.12 USD. AFlow is 0.44 (Gemini), 0.69 (GPT) and 1.56 (Qwen). EvoAgent is 3.33 on DeepSeek.
  quote: "By generating the MAS in one shot rather than re-optimizing per sample iteratively, it attains the best performance at a moderate cost."
  where: Sec 5.1; Table 1
- Evolution is a one-time offline cost and is excluded from Table 1. Break-even against EvoAgent on DeepSeek is about 21 reuses.
  number: evolution cost 9.35 / 31.36 / 59.06 / 24.54 USD per model (Table 8, summed over four benchmarks).
  quote: "The break-even reuse count is therefore 24.54 / (3.33 - 2.12) = 20.28, i.e., about 21 reused queries or deployments."
  where: App D.3
- Evolved skills transfer. Gains over init are largest with no transfer, then cross-LLM same-task, then cross-task same-LLM, and smallest for both.
  number: no-transfer +7.74 / +7.14 / +9.53 / +9.53. Panel C ranges from +1.19 to +3.57.
  setup: only GPT-5.4-Nano and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, on BCP and VITA; a small test set.
  quote: "Panel C (different task, different LLM) exhibits the weakest performance"
  where: Sec 5.2.1, Table 2
- Ablations on BCP with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Cross-task synthesis matters, and generic skill/prompt evolution (GEPA, EvolveR) beats init but not Skill-MAS.
  number: optimized 22.62; without cross-task analysis 17.86; init 15.48; +GEPA 19.05; +EvolveR 18.45.
  quote: "+ removing cross-task analysis 17.86"
  where: App D.4, Table 7
- Rollouts: more is better with diminishing returns. Selective reflection beats reflecting on everything and is cheaper.
  number: K=3 → 20.24 acc at 13.63 USD; K=5 → 22.62 at 21.75; K=7 → 23.81 at 31.18. Full-validation reflection → 19.64 at 23.44.
  where: Table 6
- Without ground-truth labels (no adaptive selection), performance drops but still beats most baselines. This is the main weakness.
  number: Full-Validation 22.02/13.10/19.64/59.52 and Half-Validation 21.43/9.52/17.26/58.33, vs Ours 27.38/15.48/22.62/63.10 (GPT BCP, GPT VITA, DS BCP, DS VITA).
  where: Sec 5.2.3, Table 3
- Multi-task evolution on a pooled validation set is mixed.
  number: GPT: BCP 20.83 vs 27.38, VITA 16.67 vs 15.48. DeepSeek: BCP 22.02 vs 22.62, VITA 64.29 vs 63.10.
  where: Table 3
- Topology lessons the evolved skills converge on. Evolution moves from a linear pipeline to a branched workflow: parallel fan-out for multi-constraint tasks, a dedicated merge/synthesis node, a link-verification step, backtracking and replanning, and merge-node re-execution. On BCP, `parse_and_plan` splits into five clue-specific retrievers, then `link_verification`, then `merge_and_decide`. The DeepResearchBench skill enforces a root → parallel branches (cap 4) → single synthesis terminal pattern with depth ≤2.
  quote: "the key gain is moving from a linear pipeline to a branched workflow."
  where: App E; Fig. 4 and Sec 5.3; Table 9; Fig. 6. Qualitative, shown for DeepSeek-V4-Flash only.
- Method details. Each task is rolled out K times. Uncertainty is the std of scores, and difficulty is the negated mean. The priority score is the average of the min-max-normalized values, and the cut-off is the elbow (the maximum second-order difference). Within-task contrast splits runs at the median score. Cross-task synthesis ranks patches. The optimizer prunes ineffective rules first, preserves the three-module scaffold, and the best round on validation is selected. The skill has three modules: Task Decomposition (what), Agent Engineering (who), and Workflow Orchestration (how, with topologies such as sequential, router, hierarchical, blackboard and loop).
  where: Sec 3, Alg. 1

LIMITS
- Authors concede that supervision matters: "its effectiveness may degrade under weakly-supervised or unsupervised settings". Label-free runs are suboptimal. Multi-task evolution is not principled.
- Validation sets are tiny (16-32 items) and test sets are 84-168 items. Differences of 1-2 points are a handful of items. No seeds or confidence intervals are given.
- Evolution cost is excluded from the headline cost comparison. It is shown separately in Table 8, up to 59 USD, with the amortization argument in App D.3.
- Ablations and transfer tests cover only two models and two benchmarks. The case studies use DeepSeek only.
- Baselines used reduced settings (AFlow capped at 10 iterations); MAS2 failed to generate executable code in the BCP case study. Baseline numbers are partly weak, so "large margin" is relative to those.
- It does not isolate whether the gain comes from topology or from added prompt detail and verification rules. Only GEPA and EvolveR are compared as generic baselines.
- Models are small or "Flash/Nano" tier; frontier-scale models are not tested despite the framing.

BUILDS ON
- Inference-time automatic MAS: ADAS (Hu, Lu, Clune 2024, arXiv); AFlow (Zhang et al. 2024); EvoAgent (Yuan et al., NAACL 2025); AOrchestra (Ruan et al. 2026); MAS-Zero (Ke et al. 2025b); MetaAgent (Zhang et al. 2025).
- Training-time: MAS-GPT (Ye et al. 2025); ScoreFlow (Wang et al. 2025c); MAS2 (Wang et al. 2025a); MAS-Orchestra (Ke et al. 2026); ToolOrchestra (Su et al. 2025).
- Skill evolution: MemSkill (Zhang et al. 2026b); Trace2Skill (Ni et al. 2026); EvoSkill (Alzubi et al. 2026); CoEvoSkills (Zhang et al. 2026a); SkillMAS (Pan et al. 2026); GEPA (Agrawal et al., ICLR 2026) and EvolveR (Wu et al. 2025b) as ablation baselines.
- Initial skill from Anthropic (2026). Related: "The illusion of multi-agent advantage" (Jwalapuram et al. 2026, arXiv 2606.13003), self-cited by the authors.

CODE: none beyond the pseudocode. Alg. 1 (App B) gives the loop. The elbow rule is j* = argmax_j |δ_j − δ_{j+1}| + 1, with p_i = ½(ũ_i + d̃_i). The initial skill text is in Fig. 5 (p. 16) and is worth keeping as an example of a generic orchestration skill.

FIGURES (one candidate): Fig. 2, p. 4, "The evolutionary loop of Skill-MAS. The Meta-Skill S(r) (task decomposition, agent engineering, and workflow topology) guides Multi-Trajectory Rollout to compute distributional statistics. These metrics feed into Selective Reflection to prioritize tasks and extract evidence E via hierarchical trajectory reflection. Skill Optimization then leverages E to refine the Meta-Skill into S(r+1)". It shows the whole loop in one picture. Alternative: Table 9 (p. ~26) shows the MAS topologies generated by each method on the same query, which is the best direct topology comparison.

PROBLEMS: The PDF extraction is clean apart from garbled math symbols. Sec 5.1 has a muddled sentence ("48.90 vs. 52.91"). Table 1 bolding was lost. Citation years are mixed: NeurIPS volume 38 entries are labeled 2026. No embedded instructions found. The roughly 85k chars noted under COVERAGE were not read. /tmp/skillmas.txt holds the extracted text, in case the caller wants the rest read.
